questions.topic: The RAG Latency Budget: Retrieve, Rerank, Generate
questions.question: What does streaming hide, and what does it not hide?
options: It hides reranking latency, but not the decode time that follows it
It hides the rewrite call, but not the retrieval legs that follow it
It hides decode time, but not the pre-generation block before it
It hides the retrieval legs, but not the reranking depth above them

questions.topic: The RAG Latency Budget: Retrieve, Rerank, Generate
questions.question: Which sequence correctly decomposes RAG latency?
options: Rewrite, retrieve, rerank, assemble, generate
Retrieve, generate, rerank, rewrite, assemble
Generate, retrieve, rerank, assemble, rewrite
Assemble, rewrite, generate, retrieve, rerank

questions.topic: The RAG Latency Budget: Retrieve, Rerank, Generate
questions.question: An answer streams 400 tokens at 15 ms per token. How long is decode?
options: About 0.6 seconds
About 1.5 seconds
About 3 seconds
About 6 seconds

questions.topic: The RAG Latency Budget: Retrieve, Rerank, Generate
questions.question: Why is summing stage p95s a safe way to budget chain latency?
options: Because every stage does reach its own worst case on the same request
Because it overestimates the tail, which is safe under correlated load
Because per-stage p95s cannot be measured separately in production
Because the p95 of a sum equals the sum of the p95s by definition

questions.topic: The RAG Latency Budget: Retrieve, Rerank, Generate
questions.question: Why run the raw-query embedding concurrently with the rewrite?
options: It doubles the embedding cache hit rate across repeated queries
It gives the rewriter an online training signal for the next turn
A slow rewriter then never blocks the retrieval legs entirely
It halves the vector index by sharing one vector per query

questions.topic: The RAG Latency Budget: Retrieve, Rerank, Generate
questions.question: What is the dominant variable cost in a high-traffic RAG service?
options: Input tokens: chunks sent per query times the daily query volume
Index storage, which grows with every chunk and its vector copy
Embedding model licensing, charged per seat on the search team
Answer cache memory, which must hold a full day of traffic

questions.question: Which cache saves the entire expensive pre-generation block?
options: The embedding cache, keyed on the normalized query text
The retrieval result cache, keyed on query, filters, and ACL
The tokenizer cache, keyed on the analyzer version in use
The prompt template cache, keyed on the assembled system prompt

questions.question: What must a retrieval result cache key include to survive a re-index safely?
options: The user's session identifier, so answers stay per-conversation
The day of the week, so a weekly corpus refresh expires entries
The serving region, so replicas never share each other's entries
The index generation, alongside the tenant and ACL context

questions.question: For which content is an answer cache valid?
options: Non-personal answers whose facts do not change with time
Account-specific billing answers that quote a live balance
Status page summaries that must reflect the last minute
Answers drawn from documents whose ACLs were just revoked

questions.question: What is the core risk of semantic answer caching?
options: It spends more embedding compute than exact-match keying does
It cannot be versioned, so a re-index will never expire its entries
It answers a question that is merely similar, not the one asked
It bypasses the reranker, so the cited order is no longer sorted

questions.question: A cache's hit rate rises while stale-answer complaints also rise. How should this be read?
options: As a success, because hit rate is the metric the cache exists to move
As a failure mode, because consistency is degrading as hits climb
As a signal to cut every time-to-live to zero until the reports stop
As evidence the cache key has grown too specific to collide often

questions.question: A result cache hits 35 percent and an answer cache hits 20 percent of traffic. What is the combined effect?
options: The index shrinks by roughly half, since duplicates stop being stored
Reranking disappears entirely, because cached lists are already ranked
Embedding cost falls to zero, because no query is ever embedded twice
Pre-generation is skipped on a third of traffic and the chain on a fifth

questions.topic: Long Context vs Retrieval: Cost and Quality Tradeoffs
questions.question: Why does retrieval usually beat long-context stuffing on variable cost?
options: The corpus is paid for once at ingest, not re-sent as input on every query
Embedding a whole corpus is free, while prompt input tokens are billed
Long contexts consume proportionally more output tokens per answer
Retrieval needs no model call at all, so only storage is ever billed

questions.topic: Long Context vs Retrieval: Cost and Quality Tradeoffs
questions.question: A pipeline sends 5,000 retrieved tokens per query; a long-context design stuffs 100,000. At equal per-token price, what is the input-cost ratio?
options: 2x
5x

questions.topic: Long Context vs Retrieval: Cost and Quality Tradeoffs
questions.question: What do needle tests consistently show as contexts grow?
options: Recall of a planted fact improves as more surrounding text is given
Recall of a planted fact degrades, worst when it sits in the middle
Models stop following the system prompt once the context is long
Latency falls as context grows, because prefill batches more evenly

questions.topic: Long Context vs Retrieval: Cost and Quality Tradeoffs
questions.question: Which workload is the strongest case for long context over retrieval?
options: Point lookups across a ten-million-document corpus at low latency
Interactive FAQ traffic running at five hundred queries per second
Price checks that must reflect the catalogue as of the last minute
Synthesis across thirty contracts that fit inside the window at once

questions.topic: Long Context vs Retrieval: Cost and Quality Tradeoffs
questions.question: Why does a dynamic corpus weaken the long-context design?
options: A stuffed context is a snapshot, so every change means re-stuffing it
Embedding models cannot re-encode a document that changes frequently
Long-context calls forbid a system prompt, so freshness cannot be stated
Snapshots occupy more storage than the live index they were taken from

questions.topic: Long Context vs Retrieval: Cost and Quality Tradeoffs
questions.question: How do bigger context windows change the retrieval-versus-stuffing decision?
options: They remove the need for retrieval at any corpus size and query rate
They make stuffing cheaper than retrieval at any realistic query rate
They move the break-even point without repealing the underlying logic
They remove the lost-in-the-middle effect that motivates focused context
